title: Pluggable schedules and retry policies
idea: An extensible scheduler accepts new schedules, retry policies and job wrappers as new classes, while the core loop and its queue stay untouched.
points: Strategy: `Schedule` and `RetryPolicy` are interfaces the core only calls.
Decorator: wrap a schedule or a job to add a stop time or logging.
Builder: `TaskSpec` collects optional settings and refuses a task with no job.
Config holds defaults, such as the retry policy for tasks that set none.

hero.caption: Schedules, retry policies and job wrappers on the right are new classes; the builders only gather settings. The scheduler's loop never changes.

code.title: Extensions, core unchanged
code.caption: A schedule decorator, a seeded jitter policy and a logging job wrapper, plugged into the same core loop.

walk.text: Config sets the default retry policy for every task that names none.
Sync runs every 300 ms until 900, wrapped in a logging decorator.
Email fails twice, then succeeds, and retries with seeded jitter.
EndsAt wraps any schedule and stops it after a time limit.
Jitter picks a delay between half and all of the backoff.
Logged prints each outcome and rethrows, so retries still happen.
The core only calls the interfaces; it knows none of the new classes.

pitfalls: Seed jitter in tests only; in production, every instance needs its own randomness.
A decorator that swallows exceptions silently disables retries; always rethrow.
A policy with state, like a seeded Random, must be thread-safe or created per task.

quiz.q: What does Extensions print for sync-users after t=600?
options: t=900 sync-users ok and t=1200 sync-users ok
quiz.why: Fixed rate proposes 900, which is not past the 900 limit, so it runs. Next it proposes 1200, and EndsAt returns empty.

takeaway: New behaviour arrives as new classes behind interfaces the core already calls.
